replacement: Every animal has ideas, since it has senses, and it even combines those ideas to some degree. Man differs from the brute in this only by degree. Some philosophers have even maintained that there is a greater difference between one man and another than between some men and some beasts. So what sets man apart from the brute in kind is not so much understanding as the human quality of free-agency. Nature commands every animal, and the brute obeys. Man feels the same impulse, but knows he is at liberty to yield or to resist. It is above all in his consciousness of this liberty that the spirituality of his soul shows itself. Physics can explain, in some measure, how the senses work and how ideas form. But in the power of willing, or rather of choosing, and in the feeling of that power, we find only acts that are purely spiritual and that the laws of mechanism cannot explain at all.

replacement: Still, the difficulties that surround all these questions might leave room to dispute whether men and brutes differ in this way. There is another very specific quality that distinguishes them, and about it there can be no dispute. It is the faculty of self-improvement. Helped by circumstances, it gradually develops all our other faculties, and it belongs to the species as it does to the individual. A brute is, after a few months, all that he will ever be in his whole life, and his species after a thousand years is exactly what it was in the first year of that thousand. Why is man alone liable to become a dotard? Is it not because he returns, in this, to his primitive state? The brute has acquired nothing and so has nothing to lose, and it keeps the force of instinct. Man loses, through age or accident, all that his perfectibility had enabled him to gain, and so sinks lower than the brutes themselves. It would be melancholy to be forced to admit that this distinctive and almost unlimited faculty is the source of all human misfortunes. It would be melancholy to admit that it draws man, in time, out of his original state, in which he would have passed his days insensibly in peace and innocence. It would be melancholy to admit that this faculty, producing in successive ages his discoveries and his errors, his vices and his virtues, makes him at length a tyrant over himself and over nature.[1] It would be shocking to have to regard as a benefactor the man who first suggested to the Oroonoko Indians the use of the boards they apply to the temples of their children, which secure to them some part at least of their weakness and original happiness.
